o1.biggest_strength: It turns the migration problem into hard launch gates: zero lost hotkeys across 1,000 real beta setups, a one-step undo, and a rollout tied to ticket volume. It also gives Product Hunt its own day so it doesn't dilute launch day.
o1.biggest_mistake: The table is titled 'users who stay' but is ordered by retention rate (X's 3,740 ranks below authors' 2,470) without saying so. Most timeline rows have no owner, and the X thread and email still contain bracket placeholders and an unmeasured speed post.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add an owner and a 'done when' to every timeline row, say plainly that the ranking is by retention rate with the totals shown, and add a mid-launch trigger for pausing or escalating if migration tickets spike.

o2.biggest_strength: The dated plan names an owner and a 'done when' for every step. Creators get builds on 18 November, all carry-over fixes are due before the 1 December freeze, and pass/fail gates sit alongside measurable targets (carry-over tickets under 20%, first reply under 8 hours) and a day-4 Plan B that pauses auto-update.
o2.biggest_mistake: It assumes engineering can build the backup, the staged auto-update and the pause switch before the freeze. That is a big ask, and it is stated as an assumption rather than made an early gate. The launch-day X content is also thinner: a single post, where a thread could show more.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Make the backup and staged-rollout build a gate checked in mid-November, and expand the X post into a short thread that credits named authors.

reason: Both rank channels the right way and treat carry-over as the real risk. The second gives me owners, finish lines, targets and a Plan B I can run with my small team, and its X post and email are basically ready to send.
